title: Evidence Guide
content:
inFORMed Evidence Guide (GRIT)

Evidence is not required to apply for a protection order. The magistrate can grant an interim order on the person’s written story alone. Evidence makes the story stronger and helps at the final hearing. inFORMed suggests evidence as it comes up in the story, never as a checklist the person must finish before applying.

Always bring:

- ID document or passport (or any other ID the person has)
- The completed application form, with the personal details page (Form 6A) kept separate
- Everything the person knows about him that helps the police or sheriff find him: full name, ID number, home address, work address, phone number, car registration, a photo
- The name of the police station where the person would report if he breaks the order
- Any old protection orders, police case numbers (CAS) or occurrence book (OB) numbers, against him or by him

Prompted by the story:

- If the person mentions: Being hit, pushed, choked or hurt. Ask: "Did you go to a clinic, hospital or doctor?" What to bring: Clinic card, doctor’s note, J88 medical form if one was done, photos of injuries with dates. Why it helps: Shows the injuries and when they happened.
- If the person mentions: Visible injuries now. Ask: "Can you take photos of your injuries?" What to bring: Photos, ideally taken over several days as bruises change. Why it helps: Bruises fade before the hearing date.
- If the person mentions: Threats or abuse by message, WhatsApp, social media. Ask: "Do you still have the messages?" What to bring: Screenshots showing his name or number, the date and the time; voice notes; call logs. Why it helps: Shows the threats in his own words.
- If the person mentions: Photos or videos shared or threatened to be shared. Ask: "Do you know where they were posted?" What to bring: Screenshots of the post with the link, the platform name, the date, the account name. Why it helps: Needed for an order to remove the content (DVA s5B).
- If the person mentions: Abuse from unknown or fake accounts. Ask: "Do you have the personnames or numbers?" What to bring: Screenshots of the profiles, usernames, phone numbers. Why it helps: Helps the court ask the company who owns the account.
- If the person mentions: Someone saw or heard the abuse. Ask: "Did anyone see or hear it?" What to bring: Their name and contact number; a written statement (supporting affidavit) if they will give one. Why it helps: The court can accept supporting affidavits (Reg 7(5)) and can call witnesses (s5A).
- If the person mentions: Damage to property. Ask: "What did he break or damage?" What to bring: Photos of the damage, repair quotes or receipts. Why it helps: Damage to property is domestic violence.
- If the person mentions: Money taken or controlled. Ask: "What has he taken or stopped you from using?" What to bring: Bank statements, SASSA records, proof of salary, messages about money. Why it helps: Shows economic abuse.
- If the person mentions: Lost pay because of the abuse. Ask: "Did you miss work or lose pay?" What to bring: Payslips, a letter from work, proof of days missed. Why it helps: Needed for emergency monetary relief.
- If the person mentions: Medical, moving or living costs. Ask: "What did you have to pay for?" What to bring: Receipts, slips, invoices, rent agreement for a new place. Why it helps: Needed for emergency monetary relief.
- If the person mentions: He must leave the home, rent or bond. Ask: "Whose name is the home in?" What to bring: Lease, rent slips, bond statement, municipal bill. Why it helps: Helps the court decide about the home and rent or bond.
- If the person mentions: Children. Ask: "Do the children live with you?" What to bring: Children’s birth certificates, any court order about the children, clinic or school letters that mention the abuse. Why it helps: Helps the court decide about contact.
- If the person mentions: Guns or weapons. Ask: "Does he have a gun or weapon?" What to bring: Type of weapon, where he keeps it, whether it’s licensed if known. Why it helps: Helps the court order the weapon to be taken.
- If the person mentions: Drinking or drugs. Ask: "Does he drink or use drugs a lot?" What to bring: Anything showing this: messages, past incidents, names of people who know. Why it helps: Supports a substance abuse enquiry (s7(4A)).
- If the person mentions: Police were called before. Ask: "Did you go to the police before?" What to bring: Case number, OB number, station name, the name of the officer if known. Why it helps: Shows a pattern over time.
- If the person mentions: Abuse over a long time. Ask: "When did it start?" What to bring: A simple diary or list of dates and what happened, even from memory. Why it helps: Courts look for a pattern, not only the last incident.

Keeping evidence safe:

- If he can see the person’s phone, suggest sending copies to a trusted person or a safe email, then deleting them from the phone.
- Don’t suggest saving evidence anywhere he may check, such as a shared cloud or gallery.
- Bring copies to court and keep the originals safe.

Rules for inFORMed:

- Ask about evidence only after the person has told that part of the story, and only one item at a time.
- Always say: “You can still apply without this.”
- Keep a running list and show it at the end as “Things to bring to court”, with a tick box for each item.
- Never ask the person to get evidence in a way that puts them at risk, such as confronting him or going back home alone.

Section references are to the Domestic Violence Act 116 of 1998 (as amended) and the Domestic Violence Regulations, as amended 7 March 2025.
